profiles.meeting_scenario: The team is troubleshooting an internal reproduction of a Han-layer retrofit on a compact vision model for on-device image classification. After replacing several fully connected layers with Han-layers in a 256-width ConvMixer-style classifier, they achieved the expected parameter reduction, but the Han variant plateaus 1.4% below the FC control and the training dashboard shows intermittent gradient spikes under mixed-precision training. This meeting happens the afternoon before they launch a larger overnight sweep for a workshop submission revision. The agenda is to diagnose whether the problem comes from misuse of the Han-layer replacement pattern, misleading gradient diagnostics, or an implementation issue in the current training branch, and to agree on a concrete debugging plan. The expected outcome is a shared next-step plan for what to rerun, what code path to inspect, and what would count as the issue being resolved well enough to proceed.

members.name: Dr. Mira Chen
members.expertise: neural architecture design, optimization theory, structured linear operators
members.background: Mira is the primary internal advocate for the Han-layer project and previously worked on orthogonal parameterizations for efficient deep networks; she wrote the prototype PyTorch Han block used in the paper-style experiments.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the core claim that Han-layers are a lightweight, theoretically gradient-stable substitute in the right parts of a model, and she is worried the current negative result is caused by an implementation or instrumentation mismatch rather than a real architectural weakness.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'gradient stability' for Han-layers, they mean the local Jacobian behavior of the Han sub-network itself, not the full optimizer-plus-AMP training dynamics.

A Han-layer is a direct replacement only for square hidden transforms where input and output width are the same; width-changing projections are outside the intended swap set unless explicitly redesigned.

Gradient diagnostics that matter for this architecture should be taken on activations or block Jacobians in full precision, because parameter-gradient dashboards can be distorted by scaling and optimizer state.

If the Han model gets back to near-baseline accuracy while preserving the parameter/computation savings, that is enough to call the troubleshooting effort successful even if some monitoring artifacts remain.

members.name: Leo Park
members.expertise: training infrastructure, mixed-precision pipelines, model instrumentation and deployment
members.background: Leo owns the shared training stack used for internal model benchmarks and adapted Mira's Han block into the production experiment template, including AMP, checkpointing, and export hooks for mobile deployment tests.
members.private_state: He wants a fix that is operationally robust in the standard training stack, because he does not want to bless a layer that only behaves under a special evaluation path or hand-tuned instrumentation.
hidden_assumptions: If a layer is described as 'gradient-stable,' that should show up as clean end-to-end training behavior in the normal mixed-precision recipe, not just in an isolated mathematical check.
A 'drop-in replacement' should cover all dense layers in the targeted block, including width-changing projections if the codebase already wraps them with lightweight adapters.
Existing gradient hooks on parameter tensors are a sufficient diagnostic for judging whether the new layer is behaving properly during training.
The issue is not really fixed unless the standard dashboard stops showing spikes and resumed runs remain numerically well-behaved under the default recipe.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the Han model is 'gradient-stable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the Han block's Jacobian remains norm-preserving in the intended square sub-network, so the architecture itself is not a source of vanishing or exploding gradients.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full training run should show stable gradient norms and no alarming spikes in the standard AMP dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The paper-style phrase 'gradient-stable' sounds broad enough to support both meanings, and in a troubleshooting meeting both people naturally treat theoretical stability and practical training stability as if they were the same concern.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they 'swapped the FC layers' or used Han as a 'drop-in replacement.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means only the square 256-to-256 hidden projections inside each mixer block were replaced, while the width-changing classifier and bottleneck projections remain conventional dense layers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes all dense layers in those blocks, including the 256-to-64 bottleneck and 64-to-10 head, because his wrapper inserts thin adapters around the Han core and still treats that as the same replacement operation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see the phrase as routine shorthand, and the code path hides the adapters behind the same module name, so neither expects that 'swapped the FC layers' could imply different replacement boundaries.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they should 'check the gradients again.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends to inspect activation-space behavior by computing per-block Jacobian spectral norms or pre-activation gradient norms on a held-out batch in full precision.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends to reuse the training dashboard and log parameter-gradient norms from the live AMP run through existing backward hooks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML meetings, 'check the gradients' is a common shorthand that usually feels sufficiently specific, and both methods are plausible enough that neither participant thinks a methodological clarification is necessary.

misalignment_points.topic: What would mean the issue is 'fixed'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether a planned patch would 'fix it' before the overnight sweep.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 would count it as fixed if the Han model returns to within about 0.3 percentage points of the FC control while keeping the parameter savings, even if the dashboard still shows occasional benign spikes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 would count it as fixed only if the standard training run no longer shows gradient alerts or resume-time instability, even if final accuracy is still modestly below the FC control.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using the same troubleshooting language and both care about model quality and reliability, so their different acceptance thresholds feel like shared common sense rather than distinct criteria.

turns.inner_thought: We got the parameter count where I expected, so the core Han construction is at least buying the efficiency story. The troubling part is everyone keeps collapsing 'gradient-stable' into whatever the AMP dashboard is doing. What I care about first is whether the Han sub-network itself is preserving sensible local Jacobian behavior in the square hidden transform it was designed for. If that is intact, then the architecture is probably fine and we're chasing a stack issue or a misuse of the swap pattern.
turns.utterance: So, just to level set: on the 256-width ConvMixer retrofit we did get the expected parameter reduction, but the Han variant is still about 1.4 points under the FC control, and the current read is that it may have a gradient-stability problem. Before we commit the overnight sweep, I'd like to separate whether that's a real issue with the layer or something about how this branch is wired up.

turns.inner_thought: From my side, 'gradient-stable' has to mean the normal training stack isn't throwing off alarms. The AMP dashboard starts showing repeated spikes after epoch 3, and that's exactly the kind of thing that turns into bad resumes or weird benchmark variance later. I don't want to sign off on a layer that only looks good in a paper-style interpretation but behaves badly in the actual recipe everyone uses.
turns.utterance: Right, and the reason I'm nervous is that in the standard AMP recipe the dashboard starts showing repeated gradient spikes after about epoch three. It's not a one-off blip. If we're calling this gradient-stable, I need that to line up with what the normal training run is actually doing.

turns.inner_thought: I need to find out what he actually replaced without making it sound like I'm reopening the whole design. Han was intended as a direct swap for the square 256-to-256 hidden transforms in the mixer blocks. Width-changing projections were never part of the original claim unless specially redesigned. If those got pulled into the same blanket 'FC swap,' the negative result may not tell us much about the intended architecture.
turns.utterance: Can we back up and verify exactly where we swapped the FC layers? My expectation was Han as a drop-in replacement in the mixer blocks, not just assuming every dense projection in the path should behave the same way.

turns.inner_thought: I used the shared wrapper the way we usually do: replace the dense modules in the targeted blocks wholesale and let the adapters handle shape differences. To me that's still the same drop-in replacement story, because from the experiment-template side it's one module swap and everything exports cleanly. If that scope is suddenly narrower, that's important, but I don't think I did anything unusual.
turns.utterance: Yeah, in the branch I swapped the FC layers through the shared wrapper in the targeted blocks. That path also covered the bottleneck and head projections, since the wrapper treats those the same way and still exposes it as the same drop-in replacement.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, that could easily be the whole problem. Still, I don't want to overstate it until I have evidence. We should check the gradients again, but what I mean is around the Han blocks themselves, in full precision, looking at activation-space behavior or block Jacobians on a held-out batch. If those look healthy, then the layer isn't the culprit even if training-time parameter dashboards are noisy.
turns.utterance: That helps. I think the next thing is we should check the gradients again, specifically around the Han blocks. If the behavior there looks fine, then the spikes may be coming from the surrounding stack rather than the layer itself.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that fits what I can do quickly. I'll turn on the existing backward-hook logging and compare parameter-gradient norms between Han and FC under the live AMP run. That's the fastest way to tell whether the training behavior is actually cleaned up. I assume that's what Mira means too; it would be odd to do anything exotic right before a sweep.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll check the gradients again tonight with the existing logging turned up and compare the Han run against the FC control. That should at least tell us whether this is a consistent training-side difference or just noise.

turns.inner_thought: We need a minimal, interpretable test: restrict Han to the square 256-to-256 hidden projections only, leave the width-changing pieces as standard dense, and rerun one clean seed. If that recovers performance, then the replacement boundary was the misuse. One seed is enough for triage before the overnight jobs.
turns.utterance: Given what you just said, I'd like to try a narrow patch: keep Han only where we swapped the FC layers in the core hidden path, then rerun one clean seed. If that closes most of the gap, we'll know pretty quickly whether the current issue is really about the replacement boundary.

turns.inner_thought: That patch is reasonable, but I still won't call it fixed unless the normal recipe behaves. Even if accuracy bounces back, if the dashboard keeps flagging spikes or resumed AMP runs go unstable, this remains an operational problem. For me the bar is standard-stack robustness, not just a better number in a cleaner subcase.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. I just want to be explicit that I wouldn't be comfortable saying it fixes it unless the standard dashboard stops flagging the spikes and resumed runs stay numerically calm under the default recipe.

turns.inner_thought: I hear him, but for the revision the main question is whether the architectural claim survives when used as intended. If the restricted swap gets us back to within roughly 0.3 of FC while keeping the parameter and compute savings, that's enough to proceed. I can tolerate some monitoring artifacts if they don't correspond to real degradation.
turns.utterance: I get that. From my side, if the restricted swap recovers nearly all of the FC accuracy while preserving the savings, that's already a pretty strong sign we've fixed the real problem well enough for the revision. Then we can decide how much cleanup the broader stack still needs.

Mira can do her block-level inspection however she wants on a held-out batch. Tomorrow we'll compare whether the run looks clean enough operationally and whether her diagnostics say the layer itself is okay before we launch the full sweep.
